questions.question: Who were the Luddites, what did they want, and how did the government respond? Use evidence to explain why the label "against all technology" is misleading.
questions.expected_answer: The Luddites were skilled textile workers such as framework knitters and croppers in Nottinghamshire, Yorkshire and Lancashire who, between 1811 and 1816, broke into workshops at night and smashed machines, sending threatening letters signed by the mythical General Ludd. They acted at a time of falling wages, unemployment and high food prices during the war with France. They targeted machines used to make cheap goods, employ unskilled workers and cut wages, not all machinery, so they were defending their livelihoods rather than opposing technology as such. The government made machine-breaking a capital crime in 1812 and sent thousands of soldiers; in 1813 more than a dozen men were hanged after the York trials and others were transported.

questions.question: Explain the story of the Tolpuddle Martyrs and why it became important to the trade union movement.
questions.expected_answer: In 1834 farm labourers in Tolpuddle, Dorset, led by the Methodist preacher George Loveless, formed a friendly society to resist cuts in wages that had fallen to seven shillings a week. Because joining a union was no longer illegal after 1824, the authorities used an old law against administering secret oaths. Six men were convicted and sentenced to transportation to Australia for seven years. The harsh sentence caused national outrage, a large march in London and a petition of about 800 000 signatures, and the men were pardoned in 1836. They became a lasting symbol of the right of workers to organise and of the injustice used against early unions.

questions.question: List the six points of the People's Charter and explain why Chartism is described as a short-term failure but a long-term success.
questions.expected_answer: The six points were: a vote for every man over 21; a secret ballot; no property qualification for members of Parliament; payment of members of Parliament; equal constituencies; annual parliaments. In the short term Chartism failed: Parliament rejected the petitions of 1839, 1842 and 1848, the Newport Rising was crushed, and the movement faded after 1848. In the long term five of the six points became law: the property qualification ended in 1858, the secret ballot came in 1872, payment of members in 1911, votes for all men by 1918, and constituencies became more equal. Only annual parliaments were never adopted.
